name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis; the paper says Redis performs like Valkey and leaves it out of most runs, so the measured comparisons are against Valkey v8.1): node throughput 108x, latency at batch size 16 0.25x (4x lower), checkpoint speed 257x (Valkey 273.1s vs Garnet 1.06s), scale-out/migration speed 94x vs Valkey; memtier (1:9 SET:GET, 256M keys, 6400 clients): at least 20x higher throughput and 3x lower P99 latency than standalone Valkey, up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; the paper says Garnet is 'already widely deployed in large-scale scenarios across Microsoft'
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation run and published by Garnet's own authors (all seven are Microsoft Research); the paper is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) but is not independent. Redis itself was mostly not run: the paper says open-source Redis performs like Valkey and uses Valkey v8.1 (plus KeyDB v6.3.4 and Dragonfly v1.29.0) as the measured baselines, so the 'normalized to Redis' ratios stand in for Redis. The CPU model is not given (only the Azure F72s_v2 SKU), and the .NET runtime version and build flags are not stated. memtier_benchmark became client-bottlenecked, so most headline figures come from Garnet's own Resp.bench tool. Language is C#, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 19(2):224-237 paper; Table 1 (normalized to Redis) and Sec. 8 give 108x throughput, 0.25x latency, 257x checkpoint and 94x scale-out, and the load generator is public (benchmark/Resp.benchmark in the repo). It is not A because the paper names only the Azure VM SKU (F72s_v2), with no CPU model and no .NET/compiler version or flags.
verification.notes: The record's caveat claiming Facebook/Meta-adjacent academic co-authors was wrong: all authors are Microsoft Research, and I corrected it. The measured baseline is Valkey v8.1 (a Redis fork) acting as the Redis proxy. The C++-only search filter returned a C# project.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
corrected_fields.caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: Server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads, bounded caches), GetPutBenchmark: 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava with concurrencyLevel 64, ~8.9x) (derived from page data); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava-64, ~7.5x) (derived from page data); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x) (derived from page data). JDK LinkedHashMap LRU reaches only 13.6M/12.8M/10.9M ops/s in the same runs.
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: First-party numbers only. The exact JVM version and flags for the JMH run are not given. The server run is an old Azure G4 / Ubuntu 15.04 setup (the desktop run is on OS X Yosemite), so the figures date from roughly 2015 and an early Caffeine release. The Guava ratios use Guava tuned to concurrencyLevel 64; Guava's default does worse. Benchmark code is public (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java under caffeine/src/jmh). Language is Java, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

verification.tier_reason: First-party wiki page with JMH numbers against ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava, Ehcache, Infinispan and java.util.LinkedHashMap LRU. The code is public (caffeine/src/jmh/.../GetPutBenchmark.java) and the CPU is stated, but the JVM version and flags are not. The rubric makes the project's own benchmark code with partial methodology C, not B; there is no peer-reviewed or independent third-party source.
verification.notes: All the figures match the server-class tables on the wiki; the ratios are computed and are now marked as derived. The C++-only search filter returned a Java project. The rubric's rule that own code with partial methodology is C forced the downgrade from B.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
corrected_fields.caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: NSDI'21 paper: close to 8x speedup over Memcached with 24 threads (Segcache over 70 MQPS vs Memcached 9 MQPS); up to 40% higher throughput than Memcached on a single thread; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes (91% less); 22-60% less memory than state-of-the-art designs (abstract), up to 60% less vs Memcached, and 42-88% less memory footprint vs Twitter's production PCache (slab) system
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230R, 384GB DRAM, one 100Gbps NIC (dedicated hosts in Twitter's production fleet); closed-loop trace replay of the storage subsystem only
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Paper numbers are for the original C Segcache module in twitter/pelikan (archived at thesys-lab/segcache), not the current Rust rewrite at pelikan-io/pelikan; the Rust README repeats them as properties of 'the same architecture'. The evaluation covers the storage subsystem only (the networking stack was not modified), uses Twitter production traces, and was run by Twitter/CMU authors. The compiler and flags are not stated. The README's '40-90% vs Pelikan's own slab storage' rounds the paper's 42-88% vs PCache. Language of the current repo is Rust, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper (the abstract on the USENIX page and the full PDF) compares Segcache with Memcached 1.6.6: close to 8x speedup at 24 threads (over 70 vs 9 MQPS) and 5 vs 56 bytes of metadata per object. The CPU (dual Xeon Gold 6230R) and code (twitter/pelikan, thesys-lab/segcache) are given but the compiler and flags are not, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The numbers are now verified against the paper PDF (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi21-yang.pdf) rather than the blog, and hardware is filled in. Tier B holds, but the benchmarked code is the legacy C implementation (twitter/pelikan: 1,957 stars, last commit 2022-10-27), not the Rust repo. The C++-only search filter returned a Rust project.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A

name: KeyDB
workload: memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 (op mix/key sizes not stated on page, i.e. memtier defaults); client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), KeyDB/Redis servers on m5.4xlarge; KeyDB --server-threads 16 --server-thread-affinity true vs Redis 6 TLS (no io-threads in its TLS start command)
claimed_speedup: over 7x faster than Redis when using TLS (KeyDB close to 1M ops/s with TLS at 16 server threads vs ~130k ops/s for Redis 6 with TLS); Redis with TLS drops 36% vs single-threaded non-TLS Redis and 61% vs non-TLS Redis with io-threads, while KeyDB shows almost no decline using TLS; latency claimed up to 7x lower
hardware: AWS m5.8xlarge (client, 32 cores), m5.4xlarge (server instances) — CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Multithreading changes the concurrency/atomicity model vs Redis (MVCC-style access under a global lock for KEYS/SCAN); staying in sync with upstream Redis features is ongoing maintenance burden for a fork
caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance types stated but not the CPU model, compiler, or build flags; memtier op mix and key sizes not stated; Redis TLS run was started without io-threads while KeyDB used 16 server threads; repository has had no commits since April 2024 even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/Snapchat/KeyDB (seeded from prior knowledge of 'multithreaded fork of Redis'); README benchmark link opened directly

verification.tier_reason: First-party KeyDB blog (Ben Schermel, Sept 2020) compares KeyDB vs Redis 6 with TLS: 'close to 1 million ops/sec' vs '~130k ops/sec', 'over 7X faster', with memtier and server command lines shown and AWS instance types. There is no CPU model, compiler, build flags or published benchmark harness, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.
verification.notes: Metadata checked via gh: BSD-3-Clause, not archived, 12,504 stars, not a GitHub fork (README calls it 'a high performance fork of Redis', so is_fork_of kept). Latest main commit 603ebb27 has author date 2024-03-21 and committer date 2024-04-04; last_commit set to the committer date. The record's '61% with io-threads+TLS' wording was wrong: the page's 61% is TLS Redis vs non-TLS Redis with io-threads.

name: KVell
workload: YCSB core workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions), 1024B items, 100GB(100M keys)/5TB(5B keys) synthetic datasets, plus two Nutanix write-heavy (57:41:2 write:read:scan) production workloads, 250B-1KB items.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: throughput at least 2x the closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads and 5x on write-dominated workloads; on mostly-scan workloads comparable or better; maximum latencies an order of magnitude lower than the best competitor, even on scan-based workloads. Body (Config-Optane, 100M 1KB items): YCSB A 8x RocksDB and 5.8x PebblesDB (next best); YCSB B/C 2.2x/2.7x over existing KVs; Nutanix production workloads ~4x RocksDB (the next best); uniform YCSB E roughly equal to RocksDB (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s).
compiler_and_flags: Paper states none. Repo Makefile defaults: clang with CFLAGS=-O2 -ggdb3 -Wall (clang++ -std=c++11 for index code); README recommends TCMalloc (gperftools). Not confirmed as the build used for the paper runs.
hardware: Config-SSD: 32-core 2.4GHz Intel Xeon, 128GB RAM, 480GB Intel DC S3500 SSD; Config-Amazon-8NVMe: AWS i3.metal, 36x2 (72) cores at 2.3GHz, 488GB RAM, 8x1.9TB NVMe SSDs; Config-Optane: 4-core 4.2GHz Intel i7, 60GB RAM, 480GB Intel Optane 905P
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing architecture can suffer load imbalance; no in-memory sorted global index so scans are relatively weaker; designed around 4KB-atomic-write SSDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper. The paper states no compiler or flags, and the repo Makefile defaults to clang -O2. CPU models are not named. The repo reproduces only the KVell side (scripts/run-aws.sh, sample_results); the RocksDB/PebblesDB/TokuMX/WiredTiger runs have no published harness. Scans are weaker: RocksDB wins with small items, and uniform YCSB E is about equal (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s). The latest commit (2025-12-15) only fixes random-number generation in a workload generator; before that the last commit was 2020-11, and the 'osdi' branch holds KVell+ (OSDI'20).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "KVell" -> BLepers/KVell; paper PDF downloaded from repo and read directly

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper compares KVell against RocksDB 6.2 (plus PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on YCSB and Nutanix workloads. Not A: the repo has only KVell-side YCSB code and scripts (workload-ycsb.c, scripts/run-aws.sh), with no RocksDB or competitor harness; the paper names no CPU models ('2.4GHz Intel Xeon', '4.2GHz Intel i7') and gives no compiler or flags.
verification.notes: The claim matches the paper abstract. I made the latency wording precise ('maximum', not 'tail') and added per-workload RocksDB numbers from the body. The metadata checked out: MIT, 293 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-15 (active). I opened the benchmark PDF through raw.githubusercontent (same file as the blob URL).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: KVell achieves throughput at least 2x that of its closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, or WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads, and 5x on write-dominated workloads; tail latency an order of magnitude lower on scan-heavy workloads
corrected_fields.caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper states hardware in detail but compiler/flags were not found in the sections reviewed (intro, evaluation setup, IO design); repo's most recent commits look like housekeeping, core code dates to the 2019 paper.

name: MatrixKV
workload: db_bench micro-benchmarks: 80GB of KV pairs (16B keys, 4KB default values, 64B-64KB sweep) inserted in uniform random order, then sequential writes and random/sequential reads; YCSB load plus workloads A-F (80GB load, 1M ops each); tail latency from YCSB-A at ~20K req/s. Each hybrid store limited to 8GB NVM, with RocksDB defaults (64MB memtable, 256MB L1, AF 10).
claimed_speedup: Abstract: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (2.6x / 1.9x vs NoveLSM). Paper body: random-write throughput (db_bench, 80GB, 4KB values) is 3.6x RocksDB-L0-NVM (RocksDB with an 8GB L0 in NVM; 1.86x-3.61x across 64B-64KB values) and 2.6x NoveLSM; YCSB load 3.29x RocksDB-L0-NVM. YCSB-A p99 latency (Table 2: 405us vs 786/2080/11055us) is 1.9x lower than RocksDB-L0-NVM, 5x lower than NoveLSM, and 27x lower than stock RocksDB-SSD, so the abstract's latency pairing is swapped relative to the body.
hardware: Two Intel 2.20GHz 24-core processors (model not named), 32GB DRAM, 800GB Intel SSDSC2BB800G7 SSD, 2x128GB Intel Optane DC PMM (8GB NVM used per store); Fedora 27, Linux 4.13.9
tradeoffs: Requires Intel Optane/PMDK-class NVM hardware to realize the reported gains; not a plain-SSD design.
caveats: Code is a diff against RocksDB v5.18.3 (the README gives the RocksDB commit to reset against); it is not a GitHub fork. The main RocksDB baseline in the paper is RocksDB-L0-NVM, i.e. RocksDB given the same 8GB NVM for L0; stock RocksDB-SSD is slower still. The abstract's 5x/1.9x p99 figures are paired with the wrong baselines relative to Table 2. Reads and sequential writes are roughly equal to RocksDB, not faster. No compiler, flags or CPU model given. Needs Optane DC PMM and PMDK. License: GitHub detects GPL-2.0, but the repo keeps RocksDB's COPYING (GPLv2) and LICENSE.Apache, and RocksDB-derived files carry dual GPLv2/Apache-2.0 headers; MatrixKV-added files (e.g. include/rocksdb/nvm_option.h) have no header. Unmaintained since 2020.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MatrixKV" -> PDS-Lab/MatrixKV; paper page at usenix.org

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC'20 paper measures MatrixKV against RocksDB (RocksDB-SSD and RocksDB-L0-NVM) with db_bench and YCSB. The repo ships db_bench scripts (test_sh/). Not A: the CPU is only 'two Genuine Intel(R) 2.20GHz 24-core processors' with no model, and no compiler or flags are stated.
verification.notes: The record faithfully reflects the USENIX abstract, but the body shows 3.6x is against RocksDB-L0-NVM and the p99 multipliers are swapped (1.9x vs RocksDB-L0-NVM, 27x vs stock RocksDB). I corrected the claim and pointed benchmark_url at the full paper PDF. Metadata verified: 76 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit on every branch 2020-08-07 (abandoned). License corrected to RocksDB's dual license.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (also 2.6x/1.9x vs NoveLSM)
corrected_fields.hardware: Intel Optane DC PMM (3D XPoint NVM) in a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system
corrected_fields.workload: Random-write workload on a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system using Intel Optane DC PMM, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper.
corrected_fields.caveats: Code is implemented as a diff against RocksDB v5.18.3 (not a GitHub fork, but explicitly derived, per repo instructions to `git reset --mixed` against that RocksDB commit); compiler/flags not stated on the paper abstract page viewed; repo unmaintained since 2020.

name: PebblesDB
workload: db_bench-style single- and multi-threaded micro-benchmarks (50M KV pairs, 1KB values) plus a YCSB run (50M KV pairs, 1KB values, ~52GB user data) comparing PebblesDB, LevelDB, HyperLevelDB and RocksDB.
claimed_speedup: SOSP'17 paper: on db_bench micro-benchmarks PebblesDB gets 6.7x RocksDB's write throughput (single-threaded random writes, 50M keys, 1KB values) and 27% higher read throughput, with 2.4-3x less write IO. With 4 writer threads it gets 3.3x RocksDB's write throughput (RocksDB default config). Inserting 50M values: 56.18 vs 14.12 KOps/s (~4.0x, derived from page data). README rounds this to '6x the write throughput of RocksDB ... 50% lesser IO'. Sequential writes are ~3x slower and seek-only range queries ~30% slower than HyperLevelDB on a fully compacted store.
compiler_and_flags: Project states it 'was built, compiled, and tested with g++-4.7, g++-4.9, and g++-5' as a general build requirement; not confirmed as the exact compiler used for the cited benchmark run
hardware: Dell Precision Tower 7810, Intel Xeon 2.8 GHz (model not named), 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04 / Linux 4.4, ext4 on software RAID0 over two Intel 750 1.2TB SSDs
tradeoffs: Write-optimized FLSM design trades away small-range-query performance on fully compacted stores; sequential-write throughput is lower than competitors.
caveats: benchmark.md shows only relative-throughput graphs (normalized to HyperLevelDB) with no '6x' text. The 6x/50%-IO line is in the README, and exact numbers and hardware are in the SOSP'17 paper. CPU model not named; compiler and flags for the benchmark runs not stated. Weaker on sequential inserts (~3x slower) and on seek-heavy range queries on a compacted store. Derived from HyperLevelDB, but not a GitHub fork. The last commit on every branch is 2019-08-03 (the 2024-04-16 date was a pushed_at timestamp, not a commit).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort stars

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'17 paper reports PebblesDB at 6.7x RocksDB's write throughput on db_bench, and the db_bench code ships in the repo. Not A: the paper gives the CPU only as 'Intel Xeon 2.8 GHz' with no model and states no compiler or flags; the README's g++ versions are a build requirement, not the benchmark build.
verification.notes: benchmark.md compares against RocksDB only in graphs; its Random-Writes bars (~2.75 vs ~0.41 relative to HyperLevelDB) agree with the paper's 6.7x. I repointed benchmark_url to the paper, which states the numbers. I corrected last_commit (2024-04-16 was pushed_at; the real last commit is 2019-08-03) and maintenance to abandoned. BSD-3-Clause and 521 stars check out. I left is_fork_of as HyperLevelDB, because the README says PebblesDB was built by modifying it.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: PebblesDB achieves 6x the write throughput of RocksDB, with similar read throughput and about 50% less IO (SOSP'17 peer-reviewed paper)
corrected_fields.caveats: benchmark.md does not itself state exact CPU model; the full SOSP'17 paper likely has it but was not opened in this session.

name: SplinterDB
workload: YCSB-derived trace replay (load phase and workloads A-F, 24B keys, 100B values and a 1KiB-value set) plus microbenchmarks, on an Optane 905p NVMe SSD with memory limited to about 10% of the dataset size (usually 4GiB), per the USENIX ATC'20 paper 'SplinterDB: Closing the Bandwidth Gap for NVMe Key-Value Stores'.
claimed_speedup: 6-10x faster insertions and 2-2.6x faster point queries than RocksDB, with about 2x lower write amplification, while matching RocksDB on small range queries
hardware: Dell PowerEdge R720, 32-core 2.00 GHz Intel Xeon CPU (exact model not named), 256 GiB RAM, 960GiB Intel Optane 905p PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD, 4096-byte blocks; memory capped at 4GiB via a Linux cgroup (per paper section 6.1)
tradeoffs: Project's own docs say it is not recommended for production before v1.0; gains are specifically tuned for NVMe device bandwidth characteristics.
caveats: Numbers come from the 2020 peer-reviewed paper against the RocksDB of that time, so the current code and current RocksDB may differ. The paper gives the machine (32-core 2.00 GHz Xeon, Optane 905p) but not the exact CPU model, compiler, or flags. It is not confirmed that the paper's YCSB trace replayer is in the public repo.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos + gh api repos/vmware/splinterdb, paper link cited in README

The paper names the machine but not the exact Xeon model, compiler, or flags, and its trace-replay harness was not confirmed public, so it is B, not A.

corrected_fields.workload: Insertion and point-query micro/macro-benchmarks on NVMe SSDs, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper 'SplinterDB: Closing the Bandwidth Gap for NVMe Key-Value Stores'.
corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers taken from the USENIX ATC'20 paper's abstract/summary page; exact CPU model and compiler/flags used in the paper's full experiments were not verified in this session.

name: libmdbx
workload: In-tmpfs CRUD benchmarks (engine speed without disk I/O) run with the ioArena harness via 'make bench-quartet', which also covers RocksDB and WiredTiger. No dataset size, key/value sizes, hardware, or result tables are published.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Up to 30% faster than LMDB in CRUD benchmarks'. In-tmpfs benchmarks that test the engine itself show libmdbx 10-20% faster than LMDB, and up to 30% faster when built with options that downgrade several runtime checks to match LMDB. The README says libmdbx may be slower than LMDB on Windows (LockFileEx locking). A separate comparison bullet asserts 'up to 10-100K times faster than both BoltDB and LMDB in particular extreme cases' (excluding disk I/O), with no data behind it.
stars_or_usage: 1468 stars; README states it is 'used in hundreds of open source projects, including Ethereum'
tradeoffs: Uses shadow-paging/CoW instead of a WAL; no crash recovery step needed but long-lived read transactions can bloat the database.
caveats: Self-reported percentages with no published result tables, hardware, or compiler/flags. The ioArena harness is public (sourcecraft.dev/dqdkfa/ioarena, originally github.com/pmwkaa/ioarena). The README says libmdbx may be slower than LMDB on Windows (LockFileEx) and slower on macOS with the default F_FULLFSYNC durability setting. The '10-100K times faster' line covers unspecified extreme cases and is not a measured figure. Canonical origin is SourceCraft; GitHub Mithril-mine/libmdbx is a mirror.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/erthink/libmdbx (redirects to Mithril-mine/libmdbx), README section 'Comparison with other databases'

verification.tier_reason: First-party README claim with no published result tables, hardware, or compiler/flags. The 'Improvements beyond LMDB' section says in-tmpfs CRUD benchmarks show libmdbx 10-20% faster than LMDB, and up to 30% faster with build options that relax runtime checks, reproducible with ioArena 'make bench-quartet'. The '10-100K times' line is an unmeasured assertion about 'particular extreme cases'.

name: NuDB
workload: Insert N pseudo-random key/value pairs then fetch M random keys, at database sizes of 100,000 / 1,000,000 / 10,000,000 keys, per the project's own bench.cpp harness.
claimed_speedup: Sample table in repo: insert throughput 406598 vs 231937 ops/sec at 100K keys, 374330 vs 258519 at 1M keys (NuDB faster); fetch throughput 333443/337300 vs 34557/20835 ops/sec at 1M/10M keys (NuDB faster) but 325228 vs 697158 at 100K keys (NuDB slower) (numbers as printed on page)
tradeoffs: Append-only, insert-only design (no update/delete), all keys must be the same size; optimized specifically for random-read performance on SSDs, e.g. content-addressable storage.
caveats: The bench README labels the table 'a sample output', so it is unclear whether it is a captured real run. name: Titan (RocksDB plugin)

claimed_speedup: About 70% higher than RocksDB in data-loading (write) scenarios, with the gap growing as value size increases, and 180% higher in update scenarios; also better point-query performance, but underperforms RocksDB on range queries and has slightly higher space amplification

name: Woodpecker
workload: Single-node, single-client, single-log-stream write-ahead-log throughput/latency test comparing Woodpecker (local filesystem, S3, and MinIO backends) against Kafka and Pulsar
claimed_speedup: Local-FS mode: 450 MB/s vs Kafka's 129.96 MB/s (3.5x) and Pulsar's 107 MB/s (4.2x), with 1.8ms vs Kafka's 58ms latency; S3 mode: 750 MB/s (5.8x vs Kafka)
license: Apache-2.0 (server/ directory dual-licensed AGPL-3.0-only OR SSPL-1.0)
tradeoffs: Purpose-built as Milvus's write-ahead-log layer rather than a general-purpose broker; local-FS/S3/MinIO modes trade off durability and availability differently; project explicitly describes results as "early stages of development"
caveats: First-party benchmark from the Milvus/Zilliz docs and project README; no CPU/hardware model stated ("our test machine"); Kafka/Pulsar tuning and dataset are undocumented; no public Kafka/Pulsar comparison harness (tests/benchmark/ covers Woodpecker only); single-node/single-stream test, not a distributed cluster comparison. Not uniformly faster: MinIO mode is slower than Kafka (71 MB/s vs 129.96 MB/s) and S3/MinIO modes have higher latency (166 ms / 184 ms vs Kafka 58 ms, Pulsar 35 ms). License is split: Apache-2.0 except server/ which is AGPL-3.0-only OR SSPL-1.0 (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).
